Next, consider $X_{9}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}W_{kl}\Delta_{n}^{2}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle|\mathbb{E}[X_{9}]| \displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta_{n}^{2}\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}W_{kl}\right]\right|\leq\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{4}]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}W_{kl}\right)^{2}\right]^{1/2}. $$

It follows that

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{9}]|\leq Cn^{-2}\alpha_{0}n^{2}\alpha_{0}\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(X_{9}) \displaystyle\leq C\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta_{n}^{4}\left(\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}W_{kl}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq C\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{8}]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}W_{kl}\right)^{4}\right]^{1/2}. $$

As for $X_{8}$ , the summands above can be grouped into 6 categories, where each category corresponds to a specific upper bound in terms of $n$ and $\alpha_{0}$ . We obtain

$$ \text{Var}(X_{9})\leq Cn^{-4}\alpha_{0}^{2}(n^{8}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{7}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{6}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{5}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2})^{1/2}\leq C\alpha_{0}^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{10}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li}$ . It is straightforward to see that

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{10}]|=0. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(X_{10}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
a,b,c,d\text{ dist.}\end{subarray}}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li}\overline{\Omega}_{bc}\overline{\Omega}_{cd}\overline{\Omega}_{da}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{ab}] \displaystyle\leq C\alpha_{0}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
c\neq d,c,d\notin\{i,j\}\end{subarray}}|\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li}\overline{\Omega}_{jc}\overline{\Omega}_{cd}\overline{\Omega}_{di}|. $$

As a result,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{10})\leq C\alpha_{0}n^{6}\|M\|^{6}. $$

Next, consider $X_{11}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\Delta_{n}$ . Using the definition of $\Delta_{n}$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle|\mathbb{E}[X_{11}]| \displaystyle=\left|\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
u\neq v\end{subarray}}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{uv}]\right|\leq C\|M\|^{2}\sum_{i\neq j,u\neq v}|\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{uv}]|. $$

As a result,

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{11}]|\leq Cn^{2}\alpha_{0}\|M\|^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(X_{11}) \displaystyle\leq C\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{1}{n(n-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
u\neq v\end{subarray}}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}W_{ij}W_{uv}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{n^{4}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
a,b,c,d\text{ dist.}\\
u\neq v,r\neq s\end{subarray}}|\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{bc}\overline{\Omega}_{cd}||\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{uv}W_{ab}W_{rs}]| \displaystyle\leq C\|M\|^{4}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq j,a\neq b\\
u\neq v,r\neq s\end{subarray}}|\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{uv}W_{ab}W_{rs}]| \displaystyle\leq C\|M\|^{4}\left(\sum_{i,j,a,b\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}W_{ab}^{2}]+\sum_{i,j,b\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}W_{jb}^{2}]+\sum_{i,j\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{4}]\right). $$

As a result,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{11})\leq C\|M\|^{4}(n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{3}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{2}\alpha_{0})\leq Cn^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{12}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\Delta_{n}\overline{\Omega}_{li}$ . Computations in this case are exactly equivalent to those for $X_{11}$ , so we obtain:

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{12}]|\leq Cn^{2}\alpha_{0}\|M\|^{2}. $$

and

$$ \text{Var}(X_{12})\leq C\|M\|^{4}(n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{3}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{2}\alpha_{0})\leq Cn^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{13}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\Delta_{n}^{2}$ . We have for the mean:

$$ \displaystyle|\mathbb{E}[X_{13}]| \displaystyle\leq\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}|\overline{\Omega}_{jk}|\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}\Delta_{n}^{2}]\leq\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}|\overline{\Omega}_{jk}|\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}]^{1/2}E[\Delta_{n}^{4}]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq Cn^{4}\|M\|\alpha_{0}^{1/2}E[\Delta_{n}^{4}]^{1/2}. $$

It follows that

Furthermore,

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(X_{13}) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}\\
a,b,c,d\text{ dist.}\end{subarray}}W_{ij}W_{ab}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{bc}\Delta_{n}^{4}\right]\leq Cn^{4}\|M\|^{2}\sum_{i\neq j,a\neq b}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}W_{ab}\Delta_{n}^{4}] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{4}\|M\|^{2}\sum_{i\neq j,a\neq b}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}W_{ab}^{2}]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{8}]^{1/2}\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{2}\sum_{i\neq j,a\neq b}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}W_{ab}^{2}]^{1/2} \displaystyle\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{2}\left(\sum_{i,j,a,b\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}[W_{ab}^{2}]^{1/2}+\sum_{i,j,b\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{2}]^{1/2}\mathbb{E}[W_{jb}^{2}]^{1/2}+\right. \displaystyle\left.\sum_{i,j\text{ dist.}}\mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^{4}]^{1/2}\right). $$

As a result,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{13})\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{2}(n^{4}\alpha_{0}+n^{3}\alpha_{0}+n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{1/2})\leq Cn^{4}\alpha_{0}^{3}\|M\|^{2}. $$

Next, consider $X_{14}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\Delta_{n}^{2}$ . Computations in this case are exactly equivalent to those for $X_{13}$ , so we obtain:

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{14}]|\leq Cn^{2}\alpha_{0}^{3/2}\|M\|. $$

and

$$ \text{Var}(X_{14})\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{2}(n^{4}\alpha_{0}+n^{3}\alpha_{0}+n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{1/2})\leq Cn^{4}\alpha_{0}^{3}\|M\|^{2}. $$

Next, consider $X_{15}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}W_{ij}\Delta_{n}^{3}$ . Using the definition of $\Delta_{n}$ , note that

$$ X_{15}=(n-2)(n-3)\Delta_{n}^{3}\sum_{i\neq j}W_{ij}=-n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\Delta_{n}^{4}. $$

It follows that

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{15}]|\leq n^{4}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{4}]\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}. $$

and

$$ \text{Var}(X_{15})\leq n^{8}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{8}]\leq C\alpha_{0}^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{16}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li}$ . This is a non-stochastic term, whose variance is zero. We the focus on deriving a lower bound for $\mathbb{E}[X_{16}]=X_{16}$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle X_{16} \displaystyle=\sum_{i,j,k,l}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li}-\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ not dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li} \displaystyle=\text{Tr}(\overline{\Omega}^{4})-\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ not dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\overline{\Omega}_{li} \displaystyle=\text{Tr}(\overline{\Omega}^{4})-O\bigl(n^{3}\|M\|^{4}\bigr), $$

where the last equality comes from (F.4) and the observation that $(i,j,k,l)$ has at most 3 distinct values in this sum. In the derivation of (F.4), we have seen that $\overline{\Omega}_{ij}=\pi_{i}^{\prime}P\pi_{j}-\alpha_{1}=\pi_{i}^{\prime}\overline{M}\pi_{j}$ , where $\overline{M}=P-\alpha_{1}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}=M+(\alpha_{0}-\alpha_{1}){\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}$ . This implies that

$$ \overline{\Omega}=\Pi\overline{M}\Pi^{\prime}. $$

Recall that $G=n^{-1}\Pi^{\prime}\Pi$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\text{Tr}(\overline{\Omega}^{4}) \displaystyle=\text{Tr}((\Pi\overline{M}\Pi^{\prime})^{4})=n^{4}\text{Tr}((G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2})^{4}) \displaystyle=n^{4}\|(G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2})^{2}\|_{F}^{2} \displaystyle\asymp n^{4}\|(G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2})^{2}\|^{2} \displaystyle\asymp n^{4}\|G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2}\|^{4}. $$

Note that $\|G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2}\|\leq\|\overline{M}\|\|G\|$ . Additionally, $\|\overline{M}\|\leq\|G^{-1}\|\|G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2}\|$ . By the definition of $G$ and our assumption (3.4), $\|G\|\leq C$ and $\|G^{-1}\|\leq C$ . It follows that $\|G^{1/2}\overline{M}G^{1/2}\|\asymp\|\overline{M}\|$ . We thus have

$$ \text{Tr}(\overline{\Omega}^{4})\asymp n^{4}\|\overline{M}\|^{4}=n^{4}\|M+(\alpha_{0}-\alpha_{1}){\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|^{4}. $$

Recall now from (F.3) that $|\alpha_{0}-\alpha_{1}|=O(n^{-1}\|M\|)$ . Hence, by Weyl’s inequality

$$ \displaystyle\left|\|\overline{M}\|-\|M\|\right|\leq K|\alpha_{0}-\alpha_{1}|\leq\frac{CK\|M\|}{n}, $$

which implies that $\|\overline{M}\|\asymp\|M\|$ , so $\text{Tr}(\overline{\Omega}^{4})\asymp n^{4}\|M\|^{4}$ . Plugging it into (F.42) gives

$$ X_{16}=\mathbb{E}[X_{16}]\asymp n^{4}\|M\|^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{17}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\Delta_{n}$ . It is straightforward to see that

$$ \mathbb{E}[X_{17}]=0. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{17})\leq\left(\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\right)^{2}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{2}]\leq C\alpha_{0}n^{6}\|M\|^{6}. $$

Next, consider $X_{18}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\Delta_{n}^{2}$ . We first note that $X_{18}=(n-3)\Delta_{n}^{2}\sum_{i,j,k\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}$ . Hence,

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{18}]|\leq\frac{C\alpha_{0}}{n}\left|\sum_{i,j,k\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{jk}\right|\leq C\alpha_{0}n^{2}\|M\|^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{18})\leq n^{2}\left(\sum_{i,j,k\text{ dist.}}\tilde{\Omega}_{ij}\tilde{\Omega}_{jk}\right)^{2}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{4}]\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}n^{4}\|M\|^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{19}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\Delta_{n}^{2}$ . We have

$$ |\mathbb{E}[X_{19}]|\leq\frac{C\alpha_{0}}{n^{2}}\left|\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\overline{\Omega}_{kl}\right|\leq C\alpha_{0}n^{2}\|M\|^{2}. $$

Furthermore,

$$ \text{Var}(X_{19})\leq\left(\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\tilde{\Omega}_{ij}\tilde{\Omega}_{kl}\right)^{2}\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{n}^{4}]\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}n^{4}\|M\|^{4}. $$

Next, consider $X_{20}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}\Delta_{n}^{3}$ . Notice that

$$ \displaystyle X_{20} \displaystyle=\Delta_{n}^{3}(n-2)(n-3)\sum_{i\neq j}\overline{\Omega}_{ij}=\Delta_{n}^{3}(n-2)(n-3)\left(\sum_{i\neq j}\Omega_{ij}-n(n-1)\alpha_{1}\right)=0. $$

It follows that

$$ \mathbb{E}[X_{20}]=0, $$

and

$$ \text{Var}(X_{20})=0. $$

Next, consider $X_{21}=\sum_{i,j,k,l\text{ dist.}}\Delta_{n}^{4}$ . Note that $X_{21}=n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)\Delta_{n}^{4}$ . As a result,

$$ \mathbb{E}[X_{21}]\leq C\alpha_{0}^{2}, $$

and

$$ \text{Var}(X_{21})\leq C\alpha_{0}^{4}. $$

Mean and variance of $Q_{n}/(2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2})$ . We use the results stored in Table 3 in order to provide a lower bound for $\mathbb{E}[Q_{n}/(2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2})]$ and an upper bound for $\text{Var}(Q_{n}/(2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2}))$ . Recall that we defined

$$ \tau_{n}=\left(\frac{n\|M\|^{2}}{\alpha_{0}}\right)^{2}. $$

We obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Q_{n}}{2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2}}\right] \displaystyle\asymp n^{4}\|M\|^{4}+O(n^{1/2}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{2}\alpha_{0}\|M\|^{2}+n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{3/2}\|M\|) \displaystyle\asymp\tau_{n}\left(1+O\left(\frac{1}{n^{3/2}\tau_{n}}+\frac{1}{n\tau_{n}^{1/2}}+\frac{1}{n^{1/2}\tau_{n}^{3/4}}\right)\right). $$

Similarly, we observe that

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}\left(\frac{Q_{n}}{2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=O\left(\frac{n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{4}+n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{3}\|M\|^{2}+n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}\|M\|^{4}+n^{6}\alpha_{0}\|M\|^{6}}{n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{4}}\right) \displaystyle=O\left(1+\frac{\tau_{n}^{1/2}}{n}+\frac{\tau_{n}}{n^{2}}+\frac{\tau_{n}^{3/2}}{n}\right). $$

Assuming that $\tau_{n}\geq C$ , then we can write

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Q_{n}}{2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2}}\right]\asymp\tau_{n},\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathrm{Var}\left(\frac{Q_{n}}{2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2}}\right)=O\left(1+\frac{\tau_{n}^{3/2}}{n}\right). $$

Mean and variance of $\psi_{n}^{SQ}$ . Recall that

$$ \psi_{n}^{SQ}=\frac{Q_{n}}{2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\hat{\alpha}_{n}^{2}}. $$

In the sequel, we let $Z_{n}^{*}=Q_{n}/(2\sqrt{2}n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{2})$ for ease of notation. First, we compute a lower bound on the mean of $\psi_{n}^{SQ}$ . Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{n}^{SQ}] \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}Z_{n}^{*}\right]\geq\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]+2\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)Z_{n}^{*}\right]+\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}Z_{n}^{*}\right] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]-C\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right]}\left\{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}\right]}+\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{4}\right]}\right\}. $$

Under the event $E$ defined in Appendix E, it holds that $|\hat{\alpha}_{n}-\alpha_{0}|<\delta\alpha_{0}$ , so we can derive the following upper bound:

$$ \left|\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right|\leq\frac{|\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}|}{(1-\delta)\alpha_{0}}. $$

Under $E^{c}$ , it holds that

$$ \left|\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right|\leq Cn^{2}. $$

We thus have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{4}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+C\alpha_{0}^{-2}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n})^{2}] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{4}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+C\alpha_{0}^{-2}(\alpha_{0}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{\alpha}_{n}])^{2}+C\alpha_{0}^{-2}\text{Var}(\hat{\alpha}_{n}) \displaystyle\leq Cn^{4}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+\frac{C}{(n-1)^{2}}+\frac{C}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}\leq\frac{C}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}=o(1). $$

Similarly,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{4}\right] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{8}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+C\alpha_{0}^{-4}\mathbb{E}[(\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n})^{4}] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{8}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+C\alpha_{0}^{-4}\mathbb{E}[(\hat{\alpha}_{n}-\mathbb{E}[\hat{\alpha}_{n}])^{4}]+C\alpha_{0}^{-4}(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\alpha}_{n}]-\alpha_{0})^{4} \displaystyle\leq Cn^{8}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+\frac{C}{n^{4}} \displaystyle+\frac{C\alpha_{0}^{-4}}{n^{8}}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i<j,k<l\\
u<v,r<t\end{subarray}}(A_{ij}-\Omega_{ij})(A_{kl}-\Omega_{kl})(A_{uv}-\Omega_{uv})(A_{rs}-\Omega_{rs})\right] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{8}\mathbb{P}(E^{c})+\frac{C}{n^{4}}+\frac{C\alpha_{0}^{-4}}{n^{8}}(n^{4}\alpha_{0}^{2}+n^{2}\alpha_{0})\leq\frac{C}{\alpha_{0}^{2}n^{4}}=o(1). $$

It follows that, for $n$ big enough,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{n}^{SQ}] \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]-o\left(\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right]}\right)=\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]-o\left(\sqrt{\text{Var}(Z_{n}^{*})+\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]-o\left(\sqrt{1+n^{-1}\tau_{n}^{1/2}+n^{-2}\tau_{n}+n^{-1}\tau_{n}^{3/2}+\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}](1-o(1))-o\left(1+n^{-1/2}\tau_{n}^{1/4}+n^{-1}\tau_{n}^{1/2}+n^{-1/2}\tau_{n}^{3/4}\right). $$

Assuming that $\tau_{n}\geq C$ , we know from (F.58) that there exists a constant $c_{2}>0$ such that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi_{n}^{SQ}]\geq c_{2}\tau_{n}-o\left(1+n^{-1/2}\tau_{n}^{3/4}\right). $$

Next, we compute an upper bound on the variance of $\psi_{n}^{SQ}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(\psi_{n}^{SQ}) \displaystyle=\text{Var}\left(\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}Z_{n}^{*}\right)=\text{Var}\left(\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}+1\right)^{2}Z_{n}^{*}\right) \displaystyle\leq C\text{Var}(Z_{n}^{*})+C\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right]+C\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{4}(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right]. $$

Recall the event $E_{1}$ defined in Appendix E. We had that $\mathbb{P}(E_{1}^{c})\leq\exp(-B\log(n))$ , where $B$ is a constant chosen large enough. Then, on the event $E_{1}$ , we have that $|(\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n})/\hat{\alpha}_{n}|\leq Cn^{-1}\alpha_{0}^{-1/2}\sqrt{\log(n)}$ . On the event $E_{1}^{c}$ , it holds uniformly that $|(\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n})/\hat{\alpha}_{n}|\leq Cn^{2}$ and $|Z_{n}^{*}|\leq n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{-2}$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{2}(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{8}\alpha_{0}^{-4}\mathbb{P}(E_{1}^{c})+Cn^{-2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\log(n)\mathbb{E}[(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}], \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\alpha_{0}-\hat{\alpha}_{n}}{\hat{\alpha}_{n}}\right)^{4}(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq Cn^{12}\alpha_{0}^{-4}\mathbb{P}(E_{1}^{c})+Cn^{-4}\alpha_{0}^{-2}\log(n)^{2}\mathbb{E}[(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}]. $$

So we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\text{Var}(\psi_{n}^{SQ}) \displaystyle\leq C\text{Var}(Z_{n}^{*})+Cn^{-2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\log(n)\mathbb{E}[(Z_{n}^{*})^{2}]+o(1) \displaystyle\leq C\text{Var}(Z_{n}^{*})+Cn^{-2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\log(n)\mathbb{E}[(Z_{n}^{*})]^{2}+o(1). $$

Recall from (F.58) that when $\tau_{n}\geq C$ , $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n}^{*}]\asymp\tau_{n}$ and $\text{Var}(Z_{n}^{*})=O(1+n^{-1}\tau_{n}^{3/2})$ . It follows that

$$ \text{Var}(\psi_{n}^{SQ})=O\left(1+\frac{\tau_{n}^{3/2}}{n}+\frac{\log(n)\tau_{n}^{2}}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}\right). $$

∎

## Appendix G Proof of Corollary 3.2

Let $\psi^{DC}_{n}$ denote the degree test statistic as in the proof of Theorem 3.2. Let $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and $q_{\epsilon}$ be the $(1-\epsilon)$ -quantile of the standard normal distribution.

Under the alternative hypothesis, we suppose that $\delta_{n}\to\infty$ . It follows from Theorem 3.2 that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]\geq c_{1}\delta_{n},\quad\text{and}\quad\text{Var}(\psi^{DC}_{n})=O(1+n^{-1/2}\delta_{n}+n^{-2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\delta_{n}^{2}\log(n)). $$

We have, for $n$ big enough,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{DC}_{n}<q_{\epsilon}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-\psi^{DC}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-q_{\epsilon}\right)\leq\frac{C\text{Var}(\psi^{DC}_{n})}{\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]^{2}}\asymp\frac{1}{\text{SNR}(\psi^{DC}_{n})^{2}}, $$

where we have seen that $\text{SNR}(\psi^{DC}_{n})\to\infty$ if $\delta_{n}\to\infty$ under the alternative (see the paragraph before the statement of Corollary 3.2). It follows that under the alternative, the power of the test

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{DC}_{n}>q_{\epsilon}\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1. $$

Furthermore, under the null hypothesis, we know from Corollary 3.1 that $\psi^{DC}_{n}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ , hence the level of the test tends to $\epsilon$ as $n\to\infty$ . ∎

## Appendix H Proof of Corollary 3.3

Let $\psi^{SQ}_{n}$ denote the degree test statistic as in the proof of Theorem 3.3. Let $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and $q_{\epsilon}$ be the $(1-\epsilon)$ -quantile of the standard normal distribution.

Under the alternative hypothesis, we suppose that $\tau_{n}\to\infty$ . It follows from Theorem 3.2 that

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]\geq c_{2}\tau_{n},\quad\text{and}\quad\text{Var}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})=O(1+n^{-1}\tau_{n}^{3/2}+n^{-2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\tau_{n}^{2}\log(n)). $$

We have, for $n$ big enough,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{SQ}_{n}<q_{\epsilon}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-\psi^{SQ}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-q_{\epsilon}\right)\leq\frac{C\text{Var}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})}{\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]^{2}}\asymp\frac{1}{\text{SNR}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})^{2}}, $$

where we have seen that $\text{SNR}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})\to\infty$ if $\tau_{n}\to\infty$ under the alternative (see the paragraph before the statement of Corollary 3.3). It follows that under the alternative, the power of the test

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{SQ}_{n}>q_{\epsilon}\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1. $$

Furthermore, under the null hypothesis, we know from Corollary 3.1 that $\psi^{SQ}_{n}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{L}}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ , hence the level of the test tends to $\epsilon$ as $n\to\infty$ . ∎

## Appendix I Proof of Theorem 3.4

As in the proofs of Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.3, we let $\psi^{DC}_{n}$ denote the degree chi-squared test statistic and $\psi^{SQ}_{n}$ denote the oSQ statistic. Recall that the PET statistic is

$$ S_{n}=\left(\psi^{DC}_{n}\right)^{2}+\left(\psi^{SQ}_{n}\right)^{2}. $$

Let $A>0,\epsilon>0$ be arbitrary constants. Then,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(S_{n}<A) \displaystyle\leq\min\left\{\mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{DC}_{n}<\sqrt{A}\right),\mathbb{P}\left(\psi^{SQ}_{n}<\sqrt{A}\right)\right\} \displaystyle\leq\min\left\{\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-\psi^{DC}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-\sqrt{A}\right),\mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-\psi^{SQ}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-\sqrt{A}\right)\right\}. $$

In the regime where $\max\{\delta_{n},\tau_{n}\}\to\infty$ , for any constant $B>0$ , there exists $N>0$ such that for all $n>N$ , $\delta_{n}>B$ or $\tau_{n}>B$ . We will denote by $N(B)$ the smallest such constant. We choose $B\gg\sqrt{A}$ and $N>N(B)$ such that for all $n>N$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{B^{2}}+\frac{1}{n^{1/2}B}+\frac{\log(n)}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}} \displaystyle<\frac{\epsilon}{C} \displaystyle\frac{1}{B^{2}}+\frac{1}{nB^{1/2}}+\frac{\log(n)}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}} \displaystyle<\frac{\epsilon}{C} $$

Now, suppose that we are in the case $\delta_{n}>B$ . Then from Theorem 3.2, we know that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\psi_{n}^{DC}]>c\delta_{n}>cB\qquad\text{ and }\qquad\text{Var}(\psi_{n}^{DC})<C\left(1+\frac{\delta_{n}}{n^{1/2}}+\frac{\log(n)}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}\delta_{n}^{2}\right). $$

Then,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-\psi^{DC}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]-\sqrt{A}\right)\leq\frac{\text{Var}(\psi^{DC}_{n})}{\mathbb{E}[\psi^{DC}_{n}]^{2}}\leq C\left(\frac{1}{\delta_{n}^{2}}+\frac{1}{n^{1/2}\delta_{n}}+\frac{\log(n)}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}\right)<\epsilon, $$

which implies that $\mathbb{P}(S_{n}<A)<\epsilon$ .

Now, suppose that we are in the case $\tau_{n}>B$ . By Theorem 3.3, we have

$$ \mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]\geq c\tau_{n}>cB\quad\text{ and }\quad\mathrm{Var}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})<C\left(1+\frac{\tau_{n}^{3/2}}{n}+\frac{\log(n)\tau_{n}^{2}}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}\right). $$

Then

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-\psi^{SQ}_{n}>\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]-\sqrt{A}\right)\leq\frac{\text{Var}(\psi^{SQ}_{n})}{\mathbb{E}[\psi^{SQ}_{n}]^{2}}\leq C\left(\frac{1}{\tau_{n}^{2}}+\frac{1}{n\tau_{n}^{1/2}+\frac{\log(n)}{n^{2}\alpha_{0}}}\right)<\epsilon, $$

which implies that $\mathbb{P}(S_{n}<A)<\epsilon$ .

It follows that for all $n>N$ , it holds that $\mathbb{P}(S_{n}<A)<\epsilon$ . We have just shown that

$$ S_{n}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb{P}}\infty. $$

Now, fix $\epsilon\in(0,1)$ and let $q$ denote the $(1-\epsilon)$ -quantile of the $\chi^{2}_{2}(0)$ distribution. From Corollary 3.1, we know that as $n\to\infty$ , the level of the test tends to $\epsilon$ . From (I.1), we know that under the alternative

$$ \mathbb{P}(S_{n}>q)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1, $$

so the power of the test tends to $1$ as $n\to\infty$ .∎

## Appendix J Proof of Theorem 3.5

Denote by $D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1})$ the chi-square divergence between two hypotheses, where $P_{0}$ and $P_{1}$ denote the probability measures under two model, respectively. and then study the symmetric alternative and the asymmetric alternative separately. By definition,

$$ 1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1})=\int\left(\frac{dP_{1}}{dP_{0}}\right)^{2}dP_{0}. $$

Letting $q_{ij}(\Pi)=\pi_{i}^{\prime}P\pi_{j}$ , we can write

$$ dP_{0}=\prod_{i<j}\alpha^{A_{ij}}(1-\alpha)^{1-A_{ij}},\qquad dP_{1}=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi}\left[\prod_{i<j}q_{ij}(\Pi)^{A_{ij}}(1-q_{ij}(\Pi))^{1-A_{ij}}\right]. $$

Let $\tilde{\Pi}$ be an independent copy of $\Pi$ . Then it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\left(\frac{dP_{1}}{dP_{0}}\right)^{2} \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}\left[\prod_{i<j}\left(\frac{q_{ij}(\Pi)q_{ij}(\tilde{\Pi})}{\alpha^{2}}\right)^{A_{ij}}\left(\frac{(1-q_{ij}(\Pi))(1-q_{ij}(\tilde{\Pi}))}{(1-\alpha)^{2}}\right)^{1-A_{ij}}\right]. $$

We denote

$$ \Sigma(A,\Pi,\tilde{\Pi})=\prod_{i<j}\left(\frac{q_{ij}(\Pi)q_{ij}(\tilde{\Pi})}{\alpha^{2}}\right)^{A_{ij}}\left(\frac{(1-q_{ij}(\Pi))(1-q_{ij}(\tilde{\Pi}))}{(1-\alpha)^{2}}\right)^{1-A_{ij}}, $$

and further obtain using the Tonelli theorem that

$$ \displaystyle 1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{0}[\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}[\Sigma(A,\Pi,\tilde{\Pi})]]=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}[\mathbb{E}_{0}[\Sigma(A,\Pi,\tilde{\Pi})]]. $$

Recalling that for all $i<j$ the $A_{ij}$ ’s are mutually independent, we can calculate $\mathbb{E}_{0}[\Sigma(A,\Pi,\tilde{\Pi})]$ easily. The calculations yield that

$$ 1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1})=\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}\biggl[\prod_{i<j}\Bigl(1+\frac{\Delta_{ij}\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}\Bigr)\biggr], $$

where for $i<j$ we have $\Delta_{ij}=\pi_{i}^{\prime}P\pi_{j}-\alpha$ and $\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}=\tilde{\pi}_{i}^{\prime}P\tilde{\pi_{j}}-\alpha$ . Since for all $x$ in $\mathbb{R}$ it holds that $1+x\leq e^{x}$ , we can bound the above by

$$ \displaystyle 1+ \displaystyle D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1})\leq\mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}\biggl[\exp\Bigl(\sum_{i<j}\frac{\Delta_{ij}\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}}{\alpha(1-\alpha)}\Bigr)\biggr] \displaystyle=\ \mathbb{E}_{\Pi,\tilde{\Pi}}\left[\exp\left(\frac{S}{2(1-\alpha)}\right)\right],\qquad\mbox{where}\quad S\equiv\alpha^{-1}\sum_{i\neq j}\Delta_{ij}\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}. $$

Recall that we chose $\alpha=h^{\prime}Ph$ for the null model. Let $y_{i}=\pi_{i}-h$ for $i=1,...,n$ , hence $\mathbb{E}[y_{i}]=0$ . We obtain, for all $i\neq j$

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{ij} \displaystyle=\pi_{i}^{\prime}P\pi_{j}-\alpha=y_{i}^{\prime}Py_{j}+h^{\prime}Py_{i}+h^{\prime}Py_{j}+h^{\prime}Ph-\alpha \displaystyle=y_{i}^{\prime}Py_{j}+h^{\prime}Py_{i}+h^{\prime}Py_{j}. $$

Hence, $\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{ij}]=0$ . We define the matrix $M=P-\alpha\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}$ . For all $i\in\llbracket 1,n\rrbracket$ , $\pi_{i}^{\prime}\bm{1}_{K}=h^{\prime}\bm{1}_{K}=1$ , which implies that $y_{i}^{\prime}\bm{1}_{K}=0$ . It follows that

$$ \Delta_{ij}=y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j}+h^{\prime}My_{i}+h^{\prime}My_{j}. $$

We plug (J.3) into (J.1) to decomposition $\Delta_{ij}\tilde{\Delta}_{ij}$ into 9 terms:

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{ij}\tilde{\Delta}_{ij} \displaystyle=(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j})+\Bigl[(h^{\prime}My_{i})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{i})+(h^{\prime}My_{j})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j})\Bigr] \displaystyle+\Bigl[(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime})+(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j}^{\prime})+(h^{\prime}My_{i})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j})+(h^{\prime}My_{j})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j})\Bigr] \displaystyle+\Bigl[(h^{\prime}My_{i})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j})+(h^{\prime}My_{j})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{i})\Bigr]. $$

Summing over $(i,j)$ such that $i\neq j$ gives a total of 9 partial sums, which we denote by $S_{1}$ , $S_{21}$ , $S_{22}$ , $S_{31}$ , $S_{32}$ , $S_{33}$ , $S_{34}$ , $S_{41}$ and $S_{42}$ , respectively. For example,

$$ \displaystyle S_{1} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\sum_{i\neq j}(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j}), \displaystyle S_{21} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}(n-1)\sum_{i}(h^{\prime}My_{i})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{i}), \displaystyle S_{31} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\sum_{i\neq j}(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{i}), \displaystyle S_{41} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\sum_{i\neq j}(h^{\prime}My_{i})(h^{\prime}M\tilde{y}_{j}). $$

It follows that

$$ S=S_{1}+\sum_{m=1}^{2}S_{2m}+\sum_{m=1}^{4}S_{3m}+\sum_{m=1}^{2}S_{4m}. $$

Combining (J.1) and (J.8) with Jensen’s inequality, we have

$$ \displaystyle 1+D_{\chi^{2}}(P_{0}\|P_{1}) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\frac{S_{1}+\sum_{m=2}S_{2m}+\sum_{m=1}^{4}S_{3m}+\sum_{m=1}^{2}S_{4m}}{2(1-\alpha)}\right)\right] \displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{9}\exp\left(\frac{9|S_{1}|}{2(1-\alpha)}\right)+\frac{1}{9}\sum_{m=1}^{2}\exp\left(\frac{9|S_{2m}|}{2(1-\alpha)}\right)+ \displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{9}\sum_{m=1}^{4}\exp\left(\frac{9|S_{3m}|}{2(1-\alpha)}\right)+\frac{1}{9}\sum_{m=1}^{2}\exp\left(\frac{9|S_{4m}|}{2(1-\alpha)}\right). $$

Write $c_{\alpha}=9/[2(1-\alpha)]$ . To show the claim, it suffices to show that

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|X|)\bigr]=1+o(1),\qquad\mbox{for each }X\in\{S_{1},S_{21},S_{22},S_{31},\ldots,S_{34},S_{41},S_{42}\}. $$

Below, we show (J.8) for each of $X$ listed above.

First, consider $X=S_{1}$ . Let $\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\ldots,\delta_{K}$ be the $K$ eigenvalues of $M$ , arranged in the descending order of magnitude, and let $b_{1},b_{2},\ldots,b_{K}$ be the associated eigenvectors. Then, $M=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}b_{k}b_{k}^{\prime}$ . It follows that

$$ S_{1}=\alpha^{-1}\sum_{k,l}\delta_{k}\delta_{l}\left(\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})\right)^{2}-\alpha^{-1}\sum_{k,l}\delta_{k}\delta_{l}\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})^{2}(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})^{2}. $$

Note that $\max_{k}|\delta_{k}|=\|M\|$ , where $\|M\|$ is the operator norm of $M$ . Therefore,

$$ |S_{1}|\leq\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}\left[\sum_{k,l}\left(\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})\right)^{2}+\sum_{k,l}\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})^{2}(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})^{2}\right]. $$

In addition, for any $i\in\llbracket 1,n\rrbracket$ and $k\in\llbracket 1,K\rrbracket$ , by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we have $(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})^{2}\leq\|y_{i}\|^{2}_{2}\|b_{k}\|^{2}_{2}=\|y_{i}\|^{2}_{2}\leq\|y_{i}\|_{1}\leq 2$ , given that $\|y_{i}\|_{\infty}\leq 1$ and that $\|y_{i}\|_{1}\leq\|\pi_{i}\|_{1}+\|h\|_{1}\leq 2$ . It follows that

$$ |S_{1}|\leq 4n\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}+R_{1}, $$

where

$$ R_{1}\equiv\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}\max_{k,l}\left(\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})\right)^{2}. $$

To bound $R_{1}$ , we fix a tuple $(k,l)$ and provide an upper bound for $Y_{kl}:=\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})$ . Note that $Y_{kl}$ is a sum of independent, zero-mean random variables. In addition, $|(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}b_{l})|\leq\|y_{i}\|_{2}\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|_{2}\leq 2$ . We can apply Hoeffding’s inequality, for any $t>0$ :

$$ \mathbb{P}(|Y_{kl}|>t)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{2t^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2\|y_{i}\|_{2}\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|_{2})^{2}}\right)=2\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{8n}\right). $$

Hence, denoting $Y_{*}:=\max_{k,l}|Y_{kl}|$ , we have

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(Y_{*}>t\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcup_{k,l}\{|Y_{kl}|>t\}\right)\leq\sum_{k,l}\mathbb{P}(|Y_{kl}|>t)\leq 2K^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}}{8n}\right). $$

It follows that, for any $t>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}(R_{1}>t)=\mathbb{P}\left(Y^{*}>\frac{\sqrt{t\alpha}}{K\|M\|}\right)\leq 2K^{2}\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha t}{8nK^{2}\|M\|^{2}}\right). $$

We now use (J.9) and (J.10) to bound $\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{1}|)]$ . For any non-negative variable $X$ , it follows from integration by part that $\mathbb{E}[\exp(X)]=1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\prime}\mathbb{P}(X>t)dt$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{1}|)\bigr] \displaystyle\leq e^{4c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}}\cdot\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}R_{1})\bigr] \displaystyle\leq e^{4c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\prime}\mathbb{P}\left(R_{1}>c_{\alpha}^{-1}t\right)dt\right] \displaystyle\leq e^{4c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}2e^{-\bigl(\frac{\alpha}{8c_{\alpha}nK^{2}\|M\|^{2}}-1\bigr)t}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}dt}\right]. $$

In our assumption, $\beta_{n}\to 0$ , which implies that

$$ n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}\to 0. $$

It follows that $e^{4c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K^{2}\|M\|^{2}}=\exp(o(1))=1+o(1)$ . Also, for $n$ big enough, $\frac{\alpha}{8c_{\alpha}nK^{2}\|M\|^{2}}-1>0$ . Furthermore, we note that for any value $z>0$ , $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-zt}dt=z^{-1}$ . Combining the above gives

$$ \mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{1}|)\bigr]\leq e^{4c_{\alpha}K^{2}n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}}\left(1+\frac{16c_{\alpha}K^{2}n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}}{1-8c_{\alpha}K^{2}n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}}\right)=1+o(1). $$

This proves (J.8) for $X=S_{1}$ .

Second, consider $X=S_{21}$ (the analysis of $S_{22}$ is similar and thus omitted). We define a unit-norm vector $u=\|Mh\|^{-1}(Mh)$ . Then,

$$ S_{21}=\alpha^{-1}(n-1)\|Mh\|^{2}\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u). $$

The variables $\{(y_{i}^{\prime}u)(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)\}_{1\leq i\leq n}$ are independent, with $|(y_{i}^{\prime}u)(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)|\leq\|y_{i}\|\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|$ . We have seen that $\|y_{i}\|^{2}\leq 2$ and $\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|^{2}\leq 2$ . It follows that $|(y_{i}^{\prime}u)(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)|\leq 2$ . Applying Hoeffding’s inequality, we obtain that, for any $t>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|S_{21}|>t) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i}(y_{i}u)(\tilde{y}_{i}u)\right|>\frac{t\alpha}{(n-1)\|Mh\|^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}\alpha^{2}}{8n(n-1)^{2}\|Mh\|^{4}}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t^{2}\alpha^{2}}{8n^{3}\|Mh\|^{4}}\right). $$

Our assumption $\beta_{n}\to 0$ implies that

$$ n^{3}\alpha^{-2}\|Mh\|^{4}\to 0. $$

Furthermore, for $z>0$ , we have $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-zt^{2}+t}\leq\sqrt{2\pi z^{-1}}e^{(4z)^{-1}}$ . Combining these gives

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{21}|)\bigr] \displaystyle=1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\prime}\mathbb{P}\left(|S_{21}|>c_{\alpha}^{-1}t\right)dt \displaystyle\leq 1+\int_{0}^{\infty}2e^{-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{8{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}c_{\alpha}^{2}}n^{3}\|Mh\|^{4}}t^{2}+\,t}dt \displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\leq 1+2\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{8c_{\alpha}^{2}n^{3}\alpha^{-2}\|Mh\|^{4}}\exp\left(-2c_{\alpha}^{2}n^{3}\alpha^{-2}\|Mh\|^{4}\right)} \displaystyle=1+o(1). $$

This proves (J.8) for $X=S_{21}$ .

Next, consider $S_{31}$ (the analyses of $S_{32}$ - $S_{34}$ are similar and omitted). Recall that $M=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\delta_{k}b_{k}b_{k}^{\prime}$ is the eigen-decomposition of $M$ ; additionally, we have defined $u=\|Mh\|^{-1}(Mh)$ . It follows that

$$ \displaystyle S_{31} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|\sum_{i\neq j}(y_{i}^{\prime}My_{j})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u) \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|\sum_{i\neq j}\biggl[\sum_{k}\delta_{k}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(y_{j}^{\prime}b_{k})\biggr](\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u) \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|\sum_{k}\delta_{k}\biggl[\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)\biggr]\biggl[\sum_{j}(y_{j}^{\prime}b_{k})\biggr] \displaystyle\qquad-\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|\sum_{k}\delta_{k}\biggl[\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})^{2}(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)\biggr]. $$

We have seen that $\|b_{i}\|^{2}=1$ , $\|y_{i}\|^{2}\leq 2$ , $\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|\leq 2$ , $\|u\|=1$ , and $|\delta_{k}|\leq\|M\|$ . It follows that

$$ |S_{31}|\leq R_{31}+2\sqrt{2}\,n\alpha^{-1}K\|M\|\|Mh\|, $$

where

$$ R_{31}:=\alpha^{-1}\|M\|\|Mh\|K\max_{k}Z_{k},\qquad\mbox{with}\quad Z_{k}=\biggl[\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)\biggr]\biggl[\sum_{j}(y_{j}^{\prime}b_{k})\biggr]. $$

We can derive the tail probability bound for $Z_{k}$ : Since $|y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k}|\leq\|y_{i}\|\leq\sqrt{2}$ and $|\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u|\leq\|\tilde{y}_{i}\|\leq\sqrt{2}$ , the Hoeffding’s inequality yields that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|Z_{k}|>t) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}b_{k})(\tilde{y}_{i}^{\prime}u)\right|>\sqrt{t}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{j}(y_{j}^{\prime}b_{k})\right|>\sqrt{t}\right) \displaystyle\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{t}{8n}\right)+2\exp\left(-\frac{t}{4n}\right)\leq 4\exp\left(-\frac{t}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}8}n}\right). $$

We thus have

$$ \mathbb{P}(|R_{31}|>t)=\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{k}Z_{k}>\frac{t\alpha}{K\|M\|\|Mh\|}\right)\leq 4K\exp\left(-\frac{t\alpha}{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}8}nK\|M\|\|Mh\|}\right). $$

We apply (J.16)-(J.17) to bound $\mathbb{E}[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{31}|)]$ . Our assumption $\beta_{n}\to 0$ ensures that $n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|^{2}~\to~0$ . Note that $\|Mh\|\leq\|M\|\|h\|\leq\|M\|\sqrt{\|h\|_{1}\|h\|_{\infty}}\leq\|M\|$ . It follows that

$$ n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|\|Mh\|\to 0. $$

We then mimic the proof of (J.11) to get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{31}|)\bigr] \displaystyle\leq e^{2\sqrt{2}c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K\|M\|\|Mh\|}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\prime}\mathbb{P}\left(|R_{31}|>c_{\alpha}^{-1}t\right)dt\right] \displaystyle\leq e^{2\sqrt{2}c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K\|M\|\|Mh\|}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}4Ke^{-\bigl(\frac{\alpha}{4c_{\alpha}nK\|M\|\|Mh\|}-1\bigr)t}\right] \displaystyle\leq e^{2\sqrt{2}c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}K\|M\|\|Mh\|}\left(1+\frac{16c_{\alpha}K^{2}n\alpha^{-1}\|M\|\|Mh\|}{1-4c_{\alpha}Kn\alpha^{-1}\|M\|\|Mh\|}\right) \displaystyle=1+o(1). $$

This proves (J.8) for $X=S_{31}$ .

Last, consider $S_{41}$ (the analysis of $S_{42}$ is similar and omitted). Since $u=\|Mh\|^{-1}Mh$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle S_{41} \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}\sum_{i\neq j}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)(\tilde{y}_{j}^{\prime}u) \displaystyle=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}\biggl[\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)\biggr]\biggl[\sum_{j}(\tilde{y}_{j}^{\prime}u)\biggr]-\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\tilde{y}_{i}}^{\prime}u). $$

Note that $|(y_{i}^{\prime}u)({\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\tilde{y}_{i}}^{\prime}u)|\leq\|y_{i}\|\|{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\tilde{y}_{i}}\|\leq 2$ . We immediately have

$$ |S_{41}|\leq R_{41}+2n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}, $$

where

$$ R_{41}=\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}\biggl[\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)\biggr]\biggl[\sum_{j}(\tilde{y}_{j}^{\prime}u)\biggr]. $$

We apply Hoeffding’s inequality to derive the tail probability bound: For all $t>0$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(|R_{41}|>t) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{i}(y_{i}^{\prime}u)\right|>\frac{\sqrt{\alpha t}}{\|Mh\|}\right)+\mathbb{P}\left(\left|\sum_{j}(\tilde{y}_{j}^{\prime}u)\right|>\frac{\sqrt{\alpha t}}{\|Mh\|}\right) \displaystyle\leq 4\exp\left(-\frac{\alpha t}{8n\|Mh\|^{2}}\right). $$

We have seen that $\|Mh\|\leq\|M\|$ . Therefore, the assumption of $\beta_{n}\to 0$ leads to

$$ n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}\to 0. $$

Using (J.22) and (J.23), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigl[\exp(c_{\alpha}|S_{41}|)\bigr] \displaystyle\leq e^{2c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{\prime}\mathbb{P}\left(|R_{41}|>c_{\alpha}^{-1}t\right)dt\right] \displaystyle\leq e^{2c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}}\left[1+\int_{0}^{\infty}{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}4}e^{-\bigl(\frac{\alpha}{8c_{\alpha}n\|Mh\|^{2}}-1\bigr)t}\right]. \displaystyle\leq e^{2c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}}\left(1+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}32}c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}}{1-8c_{\alpha}n\alpha^{-1}\|Mh\|^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=1+o(1). $$

This proves (J.8) for $X=S_{41}$ . ∎

## Appendix K Proof of Theorem 3.6

Note: this proof requires Lemma K.1 and Lemma K.2, which are provided directly after the proof.

We start by studying the case $t_{0}=0$ . We consider a sequence of null hypotheses indexed by $n$ , where $\Omega_{n}=\alpha_{n}\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}_{0n}$ under $H_{0}^{(n)}$ . For our sequence of alternatives, we consider $\Omega_{n}=\Pi_{n}P_{n}\Pi_{n}^{\prime}$ under $H_{1}^{(n)}$ , with

$$ \displaystyle P_{n}=\alpha_{n}\left[\gamma_{n}I_{K}+(1-\gamma_{n})\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad\pi_{1},...,\pi_{n} \displaystyle\overset{\mbox{iid}}{\sim}F, $$

where for all $k\in\{1,...,K\}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{k})=\frac{1}{K}. $$

In the above definition, $\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}$ denotes the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ . It follows that

$$ h:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi]=\frac{1}{K}\bm{1}_{K},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Sigma:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi\pi^{\prime}]=\frac{1}{K}I_{K}. $$

Under this random mixed membership model, it is straightforward to verify that

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{0} \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\left(1-\frac{K-1}{K}\gamma_{n}\right), \displaystyle\|P_{n}h-\alpha_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\| \displaystyle=0, \displaystyle\|P_{n}-\alpha_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\| \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}. $$

Hence

$$ \beta_{n}=\max\bigl\{n^{3/2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\|P_{n}h-\alpha_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}\|^{2},\quad n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{-2}\|P_{n}-\alpha_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|^{4}\bigr\}=n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{-2}\alpha_{n}^{4}\gamma_{n}^{4}. $$

By assumption, $\gamma_{n}\rightarrow 0$ , hence for $n$ sufficiently large, $\alpha_{n}<2\alpha_{0}$ , hence

$$ \beta_{n}=O(n^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\gamma_{n}^{4})=o(1), $$

under the assumption that $n^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\gamma_{n}^{4}=o(1)$ . By Theorem 3.5, the $\chi^{2}$ -distance between the two distributions satisfies $D_{\chi^{2}}(f_{0}^{(n)}\|f_{1}^{(n)})=o(1)$ . By connection between $L_{1}$ -distance and $\chi^{2}$ -distance, it follows that

$$ \|f_{0}^{(n)}-f_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}=o(1). $$

We now slightly modify the alternative hypothesis. Let $\{\Pi^{0}_{n}\}_{n}$ be a sequence of non-random membership matrices such that $(P_{n},\Pi^{0}_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0)$ . Such a sequence can be built e.g. by considering $\lfloor n/K\rfloor$ pure nodes in each community and all other nodes equally mixed across all communities. In the modified alternative hypothesis $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ ,

$$ \tilde{\Pi}=\begin{cases}\Pi_{n},&\quad\mbox{if }(\Pi_{n},P_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0),\\
\Pi^{0}_{n},&\quad\mbox{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Let $\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}$ be the probability measure associated with $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ . Under $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ , all realizations $\tilde{\Pi}_{n}P_{n}\tilde{\Pi}_{n}^{\prime}$ are in the class $\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0)$ , by definition. By the Neyman-Pearson lemma and elementary inequalities,

$$ \displaystyle Risk_{n}^{*}(0) \displaystyle\geq 1-\inf_{f_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{0n},f_{1}\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0)}\{\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{1}\} \displaystyle\geq 1-\|f_{0}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1} \displaystyle\geq 1-\|f_{0}^{(n)}-f_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}-\|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1} \displaystyle\geq 1-o(1)-\|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}. $$

It follows from Lemma K.1 that $\tilde{\Pi}_{n}=\Pi_{n}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . As a result,

$$ \|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}=o(1), $$

from which we obtain that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\{Risk_{n}^{*}(0)\}=1$ .

Next, we study the case $0<t_{0}$ . Again, we consider a sequence of null hypotheses indexed by $n$ , where $\Omega_{n}=\alpha_{n}\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{M}_{0n}$ under $H_{0}^{(n)}$ . For our sequence of alternatives, we consider $\Omega_{n}=\Pi_{n}P_{n}\Pi_{n}^{\prime}$ under $H_{1}^{(n)}$ , with

$$ \displaystyle P_{n}=\alpha_{n}\left[\gamma_{n}I_{K}+(1-\gamma_{n})\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad\pi_{1},...,\pi_{n} \displaystyle\overset{\mbox{iid}}{\sim}F, $$

where

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{1})=\frac{K+1}{2K},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{1})=\frac{1}{2K}\quad\forall k\in\{2,...,K\}. $$

It follows that

$$ h:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi]=\frac{1}{2K}(Ke_{1}+\bm{1}_{K}),\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Sigma:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi\pi^{\prime}]=\frac{1}{2K}(Ke_{1}e_{1}^{\prime}+I_{K}). $$

Under this random mixed membership model, it is straightforward to verify that

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{0} \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\left(1-\frac{3K-3}{4K}\gamma_{n}\right), \displaystyle\|P_{n}h-\alpha_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\| \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\sqrt{\frac{(K-1)(K+3)}{16K}}, \displaystyle\|P_{n}-\alpha_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\| \displaystyle=\max\left\{\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n},\frac{K-1}{4}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\right\}. $$

Recall that

$$ \beta_{n}=\max\bigl\{n^{3/2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\|P_{n}h-\alpha_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}\|^{2},\quad n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{-2}\|P_{n}-\alpha_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|^{4}\bigr\}. $$

Hence

$$ \beta_{n}=\max\left\{n^{3/2}\alpha_{0}^{-1}\alpha_{n}^{2}\gamma_{n}^{2}\frac{(K-1)(K+3)}{16K},\quad\max\left(1,\left(\frac{K-1}{4}\right)^{4}\right)n^{2}\alpha_{0}^{-2}\alpha_{n}^{4}\gamma_{n}^{4}\right\} $$

By assumption, $\gamma_{n}\rightarrow 0$ , hence for $n$ sufficiently large, $\alpha_{n}<2\alpha_{0}$ , hence

$$ \beta_{n}=O\left(\max\left\{n^{3/2}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}^{2},\quad n^{2}\alpha_{n}^{2}\gamma_{n}^{4}\right\}\right)=O\left(\max\left\{n^{3/2}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}^{2},\quad\frac{(n^{3/2}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}^{2})^{2}}{n}\right\}\right)=o(1), $$

under the assumption that $n^{3/2}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}^{2}=o(1)$ . By Theorem 3.5, the $\chi^{2}$ -distance between the two distributions satisfies $D_{\chi^{2}}(f_{0}^{(n)}\|f_{1}^{(n)})=o(1)$ . By connection between $L_{1}$ -distance and $\chi^{2}$ -distance, it follows that

$$ \|f_{0}^{(n)}-f_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}=o(1). $$

We now slightly modify the alternative hypothesis. Let $\{\Pi^{0}_{n}\}_{n}$ be a sequence of non-random membership matrices such that $(P_{n},\Pi^{0}_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0})$ . Such a sequence can be built e.g. by considering $\lfloor n(K+1)/2K\rfloor$ pure nodes in community 1, $\lfloor n/2K\rfloor$ nodes in communities $2$ to $K$ and all other nodes with mixed membership vector $(2K)^{-1}(Ke_{1}+\bm{1}_{K})$ . In the modified alternative hypothesis $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ ,

$$ \tilde{\Pi}=\begin{cases}\Pi_{n},&\quad\mbox{if }(\Pi_{n},P_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0}),\\
\Pi^{0}_{n},&\quad\mbox{otherwise}.\end{cases} $$

Let $\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}$ be the probability measure associated with $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ . Under $\tilde{H}_{1}^{(n)}$ , all realizations $\tilde{\Pi}_{n}P_{n}\tilde{\Pi}_{n}^{\prime}$ are in the class $\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0})$ , by definition. By the Neyman-Pearson lemma and elementary inequalities,

$$ \displaystyle Risk_{n}^{*}(0) \displaystyle\geq 1-\inf_{f_{0}\in\mathcal{M}_{0n},f_{1}\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0})}\{\|f_{0}-f_{1}\|_{1}\} \displaystyle\geq 1-\|f_{0}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1} \displaystyle\geq 1-\|f_{0}^{(n)}-f_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}-\|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1} \displaystyle\geq 1-o(1)-\|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}. $$

It follows from Lemma K.2 that $\tilde{\Pi}_{n}=\Pi_{n}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . As a result,

$$ \|f_{1}^{(n)}-\tilde{f}_{1}^{(n)}\|_{1}=o(1), $$

from which we obtain that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\{Risk_{n}^{*}(t_{0})\}=1$ . ∎

#### Lemma K.1 (Case $t_{0}=0$ ).

Fix $K\geq 2$ , a sequence $\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n}\in[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ , and a sequence $\{\gamma_{n}\}_{n}\in(\mathbb{R}_{+})^{\mathbb{N}}$ . Denote by $\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}$ the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ . Consider the sequence of alternative probability matrices $\Omega_{n}=\Pi_{n}P_{n}\Pi_{n}^{\prime}$ , with

$$ \displaystyle P_{n}=\alpha_{n}\left[\gamma_{n}I_{K}+(1-\gamma_{n})\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad\pi_{1},...,\pi_{n} \displaystyle\overset{\mbox{iid}}{\sim}F, $$

where for all $k\in\{1,...,K\}$ , $\mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{k})=\frac{1}{K}$ . Suppose that $\alpha_{n}\rightarrow 0$ , $n\alpha_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ , and $\gamma_{n}\rightarrow 0$ . Then, with probability $1-o(1)$ , $(P_{n},\Pi_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0)$ .

Proof From the proof of Theorem 3.6 for $t_{0}=0$ , we know that

$$ \displaystyle h:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi]=\frac{1}{K}\bm{1}_{K},\quad\Sigma:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi\pi^{\prime}]=\frac{1}{K}I_{K}^{\prime}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\alpha_{0} \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\left(1-\frac{K-1}{K}\gamma_{n}\right). $$

We introduce the following random quantities:

$$ \tilde{h}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i},\quad\tilde{G}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}\pi_{i}^{\prime},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\tilde{\alpha}_{0}=\tilde{h}P_{n}\tilde{h}^{\prime}. $$

To show that $(P,\Pi)\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(0)$ , we will check that

- 1. $OSC(\tilde{h})\leq C$ and $\|\tilde{G}^{-1}\|\leq C$ ,

- 2. $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\leq c$ , $n\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\geq c^{-1}$ , and $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\geq\alpha_{n}/2$ ,

- 3. $2\tilde{\alpha}_{0}^{-1}\|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|\geq\gamma_{n}$ .

First, recognize that $\tilde{h}=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\pi}_{i}\xrightarrow{\mbox{as}}K^{-1}\bm{1}_{K}$ by the Strong Law of Large Numbers. As a consequence, for $n$ sufficiently large, we have $OSC(\tilde{h})<C$ with probability at least $1-o(1)$ . Next, let $y_{i}=\pi_{i}-\tilde{h}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle n\tilde{G} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}\pi_{i}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\tilde{h}\tilde{h}^{\prime}+\tilde{h}y_{i}^{\prime}+y_{i}\tilde{h}^{\prime}+y_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=n\Sigma+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}-\mathbb{E}[y_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}])+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\tilde{h}y_{i}^{\prime})+\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_{i}\tilde{h}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=n\Sigma+Z_{0}+Z_{1}+Z_{2}. $$

Notice that $Z_{0}$ is a sum of $n$ independent mean-zero random matrices, so we can apply the matrix Hoeffding inequality to bound its operator norm. Since $\|y_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}-\mathbb{E}[y_{i}y_{i}^{\prime}]\|\leq C$ , we obtain for $t>0$ ,

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\|Z_{0}\|>t\right)\leq\exp\left(-\frac{Ct^{2}}{n}\right). $$

If we pick $t=C\sqrt{n\log(n)}$ , then we have that $\|Z_{0}\|<C\sqrt{n\log(n)}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . Similarly, it is straightforward to show that $\|Z_{1}+Z_{2}\|\leq C\sqrt{n\log(n)}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . Now, recall that $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)=K^{-1}$ . As a result,

$$ \lambda_{\min}(n\tilde{G})=\lambda_{\min}(n\Sigma+Z_{0}+Z_{1}+Z_{2})>\lambda_{\min}(n\Sigma)-\|Z_{0}+Z_{1}+Z_{2}\|>\frac{n}{K}-C\sqrt{n\log(n)}. $$

It follows that

$$ \lambda_{\min}(\tilde{G})>\frac{1}{K}-C\sqrt{\frac{\log(n)}{n}}, $$

which shows that for $n$ sufficiently large, $\|\tilde{G}^{-1}\|<C$ with probability $1-o(1)$ .

Next, we show that $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}<c$ and $n\tilde{\alpha}_{0}>c^{-1}$ with high probability. Denote $z:=\tilde{h}-h$ . We can rewrite

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{0}=\tilde{h}^{\prime}P\tilde{h}=z^{\prime}Pz+2h^{\prime}Pz+\alpha_{0}. $$

Notice that both $\|z^{\prime}Pz\|\leq C\|Pz\|$ and $\|h^{\prime}Pz\|\leq C\|Pz\|$ . We now provide a high-probability bound on the 2-norm of $Pz$ , which can be written as a sum of mean-zero independent random variables

$$ Pz=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(P\pi_{i}-Ph), $$

where for all $i=1,...,n$ it holds that $\|P\pi_{i}-Ph\|\leq C\|P\|\leq C\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}$ . For $t>0$ , Hoeffding’s inequality yields

$$ \mathbb{P}\left(\|Pz\|>t\right)\leq C\exp\left(-\frac{Cnt^{2}}{\alpha_{n}^{2}\gamma_{n}^{2}}\right). $$

Pick $t=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\sqrt{\log(n)/n}$ . As a consequence, we obtain that $\|Pz\|<\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\sqrt{\log(n)/n}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . Hence with probability $1-o(1)$ ,

$$ \tilde{\alpha}_{0}=\alpha_{0}+O\left(\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\sqrt{\frac{\log(n)}{n}}\right)=\alpha_{n}-\frac{K-1}{K}\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}+o\left(\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\right)=\alpha_{n}+O(\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}). $$

It follows that for $n$ sufficiently large, $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}<c$ and $n\tilde{\alpha}_{0}>c^{-1}$ with probability $1-o(1)$ . We also obtain from this last equation that for $n$ sufficiently large, $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\geq\alpha_{n}/2$ with probability $1-o(1)$ .

It remains to show that $2\tilde{\alpha}_{0}^{-1}\|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|\geq\gamma_{n}$ . With probability $1-o(1)$ , the matrix $(P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime})$ has eigenvalues

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{+} \displaystyle=K(\alpha_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0})-(K-1)\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}=o(\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}), \displaystyle\lambda_{-} \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}. $$

hence for $n$ sufficiently large, we must have $\|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\geq\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\gamma_{n}/2$ . It follows that

$$ 2\tilde{\alpha}_{0}^{-1}\|P-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|\geq\gamma_{n}, $$

which concludes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma K.2 (Case $0<t_{0}$ ).

Fix $K\geq 2$ , a sequence $\{\alpha_{n}\}_{n}\in[0,1]^{\mathbb{N}}$ , and a sequence $\{\gamma_{n}\}_{n}\in(\mathbb{R}_{+})^{\mathbb{N}}$ . Denote by $\{e_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}$ the canonical basis of $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ . Consider the sequence of alternative probability matrices $\Omega_{n}=\Pi_{n}P_{n}\Pi_{n}^{\prime}$ , with

$$ \displaystyle P_{n}=\alpha_{n}\left[\gamma_{n}I_{K}+(1-\gamma_{n})\bm{1}_{K}\bm{1}_{K}^{\prime}\right],\quad\mbox{and}\quad\pi_{1},...,\pi_{n} \displaystyle\overset{\mbox{iid}}{\sim}F, $$

where

$$ \mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{1})=\frac{K+1}{2K},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathbb{P}_{\pi\sim F}(\pi=e_{k})=\frac{1}{2K}\quad\forall k\in\{2,...,K\}. $$

Suppose that $\alpha_{n}\rightarrow 0$ , $n\alpha_{n}\rightarrow\infty$ , $\gamma_{n}\rightarrow 0$ , and $0<t_{0}<\sqrt{(K-1)(K+3)/(16K)}$ . Then, with probability $1-o(1)$ , $(P_{n},\Pi_{n})\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0})$ .

Proof From the proof of Theorem 3.6 for $t_{0}>0$ , we know that

$$ \displaystyle h: \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi]=\frac{1}{2K}(Ke_{1}+\bm{1}_{K}), \displaystyle\Sigma: \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim F}[\pi\pi^{\prime}]=\frac{1}{2K}(Ke_{1}e_{1}^{\prime}+I_{K}), \displaystyle\mbox{and}\quad\alpha_{0} \displaystyle=\alpha_{n}\left(1-\frac{3K-3}{4K}\gamma_{n}\right). $$

We introduce the following random quantities:

$$ \tilde{h}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i},\quad\tilde{G}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}\pi_{i}^{\prime},\mbox{and}\quad\tilde{\alpha}_{0}=\tilde{h}P_{n}\tilde{h}^{\prime}. $$

To show that $(P,\Pi)\in\mathcal{M}_{1n}(t_{0})$ , we will check that

- 1. $OSC(\tilde{h})\leq C$ and $\|\tilde{G}^{-1}\|\leq C$ ,

- 2. $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\leq c$ , $n\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\geq c^{-1}$ , and $\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\geq\alpha_{n}/2$ ,

- 3. $2\tilde{\alpha}_{0}^{-1}\|P-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|\geq\gamma_{n}$ and $\|P\tilde{h}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\|\geq t_{0}\|P-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|$ .

The first two points can be shown with probability at least $1-o(1)$ in the same way as in the proof of Lemma K.1. We will focus on the third point. For $n$ sufficiently large, $\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}$ is the largest eigenvalue of $(P-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime})$ in magnitude. Hence, we must have, for $n$ sufficiently big

$$ \|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}\geq\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\gamma_{n}/2. $$

Now, introduce the (continuous) function with support $\mathbb{R}^{K}$ :

$$ g(x):=\left\|\begin{bmatrix}x_{1}(1-x_{1})-\sum_{k\neq 1}x_{k}^{2}\\
x_{2}(1-x_{2})-\sum_{k\neq 2}x_{k}^{2}\\
\vdots\\
x_{K}(1-x_{K})-\sum_{k\neq K}x_{k}^{2}\end{bmatrix}\right\|. $$

Notice that $\|P\tilde{h}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\|=\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}g(\tilde{h})$ and $g(h)=\sqrt{(K-1)(K+3)/(16K)}$ . As a consequence, for $n$ sufficiently large,

$$ \frac{\|P_{n}\tilde{h}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\|}{\|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|}=\frac{\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}g(\tilde{h})}{\alpha_{n}\gamma_{n}}\xrightarrow{\mbox{as}}g(h)=\sqrt{\frac{(K-1)(K+3)}{16K}}>t_{0}. $$

It follows that for $n$ sufficiently large, with probability at least $1-o(1)$ ,

$$ \|P_{n}\tilde{h}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}\bm{1}_{K}\|\geq t_{0}\|P_{n}-\tilde{\alpha}_{0}{\bf 1}_{K}{\bf 1}_{K}^{\prime}\|, $$

which concludes the proof. ∎

## Appendix L Proof of Propositions 4.1-4.2

### L.1 Proof of Proposition 4.1

We suppose that there exists an eligible tuple $(\Pi_{0},P_{0},K_{0})$ such that $\Omega=\Pi_{0}P_{0}\Pi_{0}^{\prime}$ . To show the first point of the proposition, define the set:

$$ S=\left\{k\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\quad\middle|\quad\exists(\Pi,P)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\times\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}\text{ eligible such that }\Omega=\Pi P\Pi^{\prime}\right\}. $$

Note that $S$ is a discrete set lower bounded by $0$ which is non-empty since $K_{0}\in S$ by assumption. It follows that $S$ has a lower bound, which we denote as $k_{\Omega}$ . It corresponds to the INC defined in Definition 4.2.

Now, we proceed to showing that when $K=k_{\Omega}$ , the matrix $P$ is identifiable up to permutation. Suppose that we have two pairs of eligible matrices $(\Pi,P),(\Pi^{*},P^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\Omega}}\times\mathbb{R}^{k_{\Omega}\times k_{\Omega}}$ such that $\Omega=\Pi P\Pi^{\prime}=\Pi^{*}P^{*}(\Pi^{*})^{\prime}$ . Because $\Pi,\Pi^{*}$ are eligible, they contain the identity matrix as a submatrix. We assume without loss of generality that the first $k_{\Omega}$ rows of $\Pi$ and $\Pi^{*}$ correspond to $k_{\Omega}$ pure points, one per community. The submatrices

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Pi}:=\Pi_{|\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\},\cdot}\quad\text{ and }\tilde{\Pi}^{*}:=\Pi^{*}_{|\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\},\cdot} $$

are permutations matrix. We have

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{|\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\}\times\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\}}=\tilde{\Pi}P\tilde{\Pi}^{\prime}=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}P^{*}(\tilde{\Pi}^{*})^{\prime}, $$

which implies that $P^{*}=DPD^{\prime}$ , where $D=(\tilde{\Pi}^{*})^{\prime}\tilde{\Pi}$ is a permutation matrix.

If, in addition, we have that $\text{rank}(P)=k_{\Omega}$ , then $P$ is invertible. It follows that

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{\Pi}P=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}P^{*}(\tilde{\Pi}^{*})^{\prime}\tilde{\Pi}=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}P^{*}D=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}DP\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tilde{\Pi}=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}D. $$

In addition, since $\Omega=\Pi P\Pi^{\prime}=\Pi^{*}P^{*}(\Pi^{*})^{\prime}$ , $\Pi$ and $\Pi^{*}$ have full column rank, which means that there must exist an invertible matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$ such that $\Pi=\Pi^{*}B$ . This implies that $\tilde{\Pi}=\tilde{\Pi}^{*}B$ . As a result that $B=D$ , so $\Pi=\Pi^{*}D$ . This shows that if $\text{rank}(P)=k_{\Omega}$ , then $\Pi$ is also identifiable up to permutation.

Finally, it holds by definition of $k_{\Omega}$ that $K_{0}\geq k_{\Omega}$ . Since $\text{rank}(P_{0})=\text{rank}(\Omega)$ and $k_{\Omega}=\text{dim}(P)\geq\text{rank}(\Omega)$ , we obtain that

$$ K_{0}\geq k_{\Omega}\geq\text{rank}(P_{0}). $$

Furthermore, if $P_{0}$ is non-singular, then $K_{0}=\text{rank}(P_{0})$ , hence

$$ K_{0}=k_{\Omega}=\text{rank}(P_{0}). $$

### L.2 Proof of Proposition 4.2

By Proposition 4.1, there exists a pair of eligible $\Pi\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k_{\Omega}}$ and $P\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{\Omega}\times k\Omega}$ such that $\Omega=\Pi P\Pi^{\prime}$ , where $k_{\Omega}$ is the INC. Hence in the rest of the proof, we take $K=k_{\Omega}$ .

Denote by $\Lambda\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}$ the matrix of eigenvalues of $\Omega$ . It follows that we can write $\Omega=\Xi\Lambda\Xi^{\prime}$ . Furthermore, note that the fact that $r=\text{rank}(\Omega)$ implies that we also have $\text{rank}(P)=r$ . We can thus denote by $X\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{\Omega}\times r}$ the matrix of eigenvectors of $P$ , and by $L\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}$ the corresponding matrix of non-zero eigenvalues, thus obtaining that $P=XLX^{\prime}$ . As a consequence,

$$ \Omega=\Xi\Lambda\Xi^{\prime}=\Pi XL(\Pi X)^{\prime}. $$

Note that $\Lambda\Xi^{\prime}$ and $L(\Pi X)^{\prime}$ must have full row-rank $r$ , so the column space of $\Xi$ is equal to the column space of $\Pi X$ . There must exist a matrix $B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}$ such that $\Xi=\Pi XB$ . Hence there exists a matrix $V\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{\Omega}\times r}$ such that

$$ \Xi=\Pi V. $$

Since $\Pi$ is a membership matrix, it follows that the rows of $\Xi$ are convex combinations of the $k_{\Omega}$ rows of $V$ . Because $\Pi$ is eligible, the identity matrix is a submatrix of $\Pi$ . Without loss of generality, assume that $\Pi_{|\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\},\cdot}=I_{k_{\Omega}}$ . It follows that $V=\Xi_{\{1,...,k_{\Omega}\},\cdot}$ . This shows that $C(\Xi)$ is a polytope with at most $k_{\Omega}$ vertices and at least $r$ vertices.

In the case that $k_{\Omega}=r$ , the desired result follows immediately. In the case that $k_{\Omega}<r$ , hic jacet lepus. Suppose by contradiction that $V$ has only $N$ distinct rows, where $r\leq N<k_{\Omega}$ . This means that we can write $\Xi=\Pi B\tilde{V}$ , where $\tilde{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times r}$ is the matrix containing the unique rows of $V$ and $B\in\mathbb{R}^{k_{\Omega}\times N}$ is a row-replication matrix (which admits the identity matrix $I_{N}$ as a submatrix). It follows that we can write:

$$ \Omega=\Pi B\tilde{V}\Lambda\tilde{V}^{\prime}B^{\prime}\Pi^{\prime}. $$

We denote $\tilde{\Pi}:=\Pi B$ and $\tilde{P}=\tilde{V}\Lambda\tilde{V}^{\prime}$ , and proceed to showing that these matrices are eligible. First, it is straightforward to see that for any $i\in\{1,...,n\}$ , the $i$ -th row of $\tilde{\Pi}$ is positive and verifies $\tilde{\pi}_{i}^{\prime}\bm{1}_{N}=\pi_{i}^{\prime}B\bm{1}_{N}=\pi^{\prime}\bm{1}_{K}=1$ . In addition, since both $\Pi$ admits $I_{k_{\Omega}}$ as a submatrix and $B$ admits $I_{N}$ as a submatrix, it follows that $\tilde{\Pi}$ admits $I_{N}$ as a submatrix. This shows that $\tilde{\Pi}$ is admissible.

Now, from Equation (L.1), we know that $\Omega=\Pi V\Lambda V^{\prime}\Pi^{\prime}$ , so $P=V\Lambda V^{\prime}=B\tilde{V}\Lambda\tilde{V}^{\prime}B^{\prime}$ . By definition, $B$ admits a left inverse, call it $Q\in\{0,1\}^{N\times k_{\Omega}}$ , so that $QB=I_{2}$ . Then $\tilde{P}=QPQ^{\prime}$ . Since both $Q$ and $P$ are nonnegative, it follows that $\tilde{P}$ is nonnegative, thus eligible.

We have shown that we can write $\Omega=\tilde{\Pi}\tilde{P}\tilde{\Pi}^{\prime}$ , where $(\tilde{\Pi},\tilde{P})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times N}\times\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ eligible and $N<k_{\Omega}$ , QEA. ∎
